newsitem.title: USA: Aluminum tags to dip in 1997, firmer in 1998 - CRU.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum tags to dip in 1997, firmer in 1998 - CRU.

text.p: Primary aluminum prices are set to fall by year end, but pick up again during 1998 to levels above today's, analyst Nick Mason of CRU International said.

LME three months price will fall to $1,500 to $1,600 per tonne by the end of 1997 and then rise modestly in the spring and summer of next year to $1,750, Mason said in a presentation at Alumitech, an industry gathering organised by the Aluminum Association.
LME three months officially settled at $1,638 a tonne Tuesday.

Mason believed producers were disciplined enough to keep current idled capacity shut going into 1998. Some 800,000 to 1 million tonnes of capacity is idled in North America, held by three companies, Alcoa, Reynolds Metals, and Alcan.
"Producer discipline has a lot of credibility now," Mason said.

"We project primary consumption (in 1998) to rise by a more modest three percent to just under 19 million tonnes," Mason said. "This should create a deficit in the first six months of 1998, and the market should be in balance thereafter."
Visible stocks should return to 50 days of consumption in the second quarter of 1998 and then rise only modestly.
Near-term in 1997, the market will remain in deficit up to mid-year but as the stock build subsides, the market will then move to a modest surplus.
Overall in 1997, Mason expected a 120,000-tonne shortfall in supply with visible stocks at 60 days.
Price fluctuations will be much more modest than in the past because the large funds are not so active in aluminum and producers were determined to keep capacity off line, Mason said.
